title: Presidents and Prime Ministers
objective: After this level you can compare presidential and parliamentary systems.
summary: Parliaments choose prime ministers and can remove them by a no-confidence vote, as in 1979; presidents are elected for fixed terms and are also head of state. France mixes the two.

cards.headline: On 28 March 1979, a British government lost a vote by one: 311 to 310.
cards.body: The House of Commons passed a motion of no confidence in Prime Minister James Callaghan's government, and he asked for a general election. A US president can't be sent packing by a vote like that. Why the difference? It comes down to where the leader's power comes from.

cards.headline: Prime ministers: chosen by parliament
cards.body: In a parliamentary system, the head of government, the prime minister, is selected by the legislature. Usually the party or coalition with the most seats forms the government. And what parliament gives, it can take away: a prime minister can be removed whenever they lose the confidence of a majority of parliament. That's the 1979 story.

cards.headline: Presidents: elected for a fixed term
cards.body: In a presidential system, the head of government is popularly elected to a fixed term and doesn't depend on the legislature for power. The United States is the classic case. There's a second hat, too. The head of state is a ceremonial role; the head of government has real power. A president wears both. In parliamentary systems they're split, like Germany's president and chancellor.

mascot.line: Head of state and head of government are easy to confuse. One is ceremony, one is real power; a president wears both.

questions.prompt: By what margin did the UK Commons pass its 1979 no-confidence motion in Callaghan's government?

options.label: By 100 votes
options.rationale: Far closer than that: a single vote.

options.label: It was unanimous
options.rationale: It was one of the narrowest votes possible: 311 to 310.

questions.explanation: The motion passed 311 votes to 310, a margin of one, and Callaghan asked for a general election.

questions.prompt: In a presidential system like the United States, who is head of state?

options.label: A monarch with a ceremonial role
options.rationale: In a presidential system the president holds this role.

options.label: The leader of the largest party in the legislature
options.rationale: That describes a prime minister's route to power.

options.label: The chief judge of the highest court
options.rationale: Judges aren't heads of state here.

options.label: The president, who is also head of government

questions.explanation: In presidential systems one person wears both hats: the president is head of state and head of government.

questions.prompt: Level 23 said a UK prime minister needs a Commons majority. In a parliamentary system, what can happen to a PM who loses it?

options.label: Nothing until their fixed term runs out
options.rationale: Fixed terms are a presidential feature.

options.label: They can be removed from power
They automatically become head of state
options.rationale: Losing confidence removes power; it doesn't add a role.

options.label: The courts choose a new prime minister

questions.explanation: A prime minister can be removed whenever they lose the confidence of a majority of parliament.
